\chapter{Water, Wine, and Bread}
\label{ch:la-water-wine-bread}
\hlchaptermodality{10}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name water, wine, and bread in Latin, and explain why a companion is someone you share bread with.}

Ask for aqua, vīnum, and pānis, then unpack com- plus pānis into companion.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[aqua, vīnum]{aqua, vīnum — one word worn thin, one word untouched}

\label{lesson:LA-C10-aqua-vinum}



\begin{quote}
Two everyday Latin nouns — and two wildly different fates. One of Rome's daughters wore this word down to almost nothing. The other word barely moved at all, anywhere.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{aqua, aquae} — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{water}.\textquotedblright{} Spanish and Italian kept it close to whole: \textbf{agua}, \textbf{acqua}. French, though, eroded it further than almost any other word it inherited from Latin: \emph{aqua $\to$ ewe $\to$ eaue $\to$ \textbf{eau}} — three written letters, \emph{e-a-u}, spelling one bare vowel sound, \textquotedblleft{}oh.\textquotedblright{} Compare \emph{caput}, which French similarly abandoned as an everyday word (for \emph{testa}) — \emph{aqua} wasn't replaced, but it was worn down almost to nothing while staying in place.

English kept the \textbf{whole, undamaged} word as a learned borrowing: \textbf{aquatic, aquarium, aqueduct, aqualung} all sound exactly like their Latin ancestor.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: vīnum — survived, everywhere, almost untouched}
\textbf{vīnum, vīnī} — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{wine}.\textquotedblright{} Unlike \emph{aqua} and \emph{caput}, this word simply \textbf{didn't erode much in any direction}: Spanish \emph{vino}, French \emph{vin}, Italian \emph{vino} — all close to the original. Germanic borrowed it directly and early, giving English \textbf{wine} itself. Centuries later, English picked up more of the family — this time secondhand, through \textbf{French}: \textbf{vine} (< OF \emph{vigne} < \emph{vīnea}, \textquotedblleft{}vineyard\textquotedblright{}), \textbf{vinegar} (< OF \emph{vinaigre}, \emph{vin} + \emph{aigre}, ultimately \emph{acer} \textquotedblleft{}sour\textquotedblright{}), \textbf{vintage} (< OF \emph{vendage} < \emph{vīndēmia}, \emph{vīnum} + \emph{dēmere} \textquotedblleft{}to harvest\textquotedblright{}). \textbf{Vineyard} isn't a borrowing at all — English built it at home, compounding the already- borrowed \textquotedblleft{}wine\textquotedblright{} with native \textquotedblleft{}yard.\textquotedblright{} Few Latin words traveled this far, by this many different roads, and stayed this recognizable.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}aqua\textquotedblright{} — water — then the daughters: \textquotedblleft{}agua, acqua, eau\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}vīnum\textquotedblright{} — wine — then: \textquotedblleft{}vino, vin, vino, wine\textquotedblright{}
  \item the contrast — aqua wore thin in French; vīnum stayed solid everywhere
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which Latin word for a drink got worn down almost to nothing, and in which language? (\textbf{Aqua}, in \textbf{French} — down to a bare \textquotedblleft{}eau.\textquotedblright{}) Which word barely changed \textbf{anywhere}, surviving into every Romance daughter and into English too? (\textbf{Vīnum} — wine, vino, vin, vino.) Where did the \emph{whole}, undamaged form of \emph{aqua} survive in English? (\textbf{Aquatic, aquarium, aqueduct} — learned borrowings, not everyday words.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[pānis]{pānis — bread, and the friend who shares it}

\label{lesson:LA-C10-panis}



\begin{quote}
One Latin word for bread, surviving whole across every Romance daughter — and hiding, inside a compound, one of the loveliest word-stories in English.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{pānis, pānis} — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{bread}.\textquotedblright{} Spanish \textbf{pan}, French \textbf{pain}, Italian \textbf{pane} all continue it directly — bread mattered enough to keep its own name everywhere.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: com- + pānis — \textquotedblleft{}sharing bread\textquotedblright{}}
Add the prefix \textbf{com-} (\textquotedblleft{}with, together\textquotedblright{}) and you get \textbf{compānio/ compānia} — a Vulgar Latin coinage, not a Classical-era word — literally \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{one you share bread with},\textquotedblright{} the direct ancestor of English \textbf{companion} and \textbf{company}. A \emph{company} was, at first, nothing more than a group who ate together.

\begin{culture}
English only kept the \textbf{friendship} half of this word — \emph{companion} has nothing to do with actual bread anymore to an English speaker. \textbf{Spanish}, though, still keeps \textbf{both halves} traceably related: \textbf{pan} (the bread itself) and \textbf{compañero} (the friend, \textquotedblleft{}one who shares \emph{pan}\textquotedblright{}) sit right next to each other in the same language, both transparently built from the same root. Latin's \emph{pānis} split into two separate lives in English, but stayed one visible family in Spanish.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}pānis\textquotedblright{} — bread — then \textquotedblleft{}pan, pain, pane\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}com- + pānis\textquotedblright{} — \textquotedblleft{}with bread\textquotedblright{} — companion, company
  \item the contrast — English kept only the friend; Spanish kept both the bread and the friend
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \textbf{pānis} give Spanish, French, and Italian directly? (\textbf{Pan, pain, pane} — bread.) What English words come from \emph{com- + pānis}, and what do they literally mean? (\textbf{Companion, company} — \textquotedblleft{}one you \textbf{share bread with}.\textquotedblright{}) Does English still connect \textquotedblleft{}companion\textquotedblright{} to actual bread? (\textbf{No} — only Spanish keeps both \emph{pan} and \emph{compañero} traceably related.)
\end{tcolorbox}
